Resolvent sampling and positive periodization

Original edition by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Repaired and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Original exposition: public domain (CC0); linked prerequisites retain their stated licences.

A positive partition can turn any bounded measurable function into a periodic approximation while controlling both its values and its spectrum. We build that partition from the squared sinc function, then prove the full support bound, the rectangular extension and the sharp approximation and degree estimates. A second use of the same sampling machinery turns a resolvent's exponential spectrum into a cotangent sum and an exact Cauchy-grid error. Both inversion and Gaussian regularization are retained as routes to the Cauchy Fourier pair. Section and result numbers remain stable for subsequent lessons that cite them.

Use , with complex bilinear distribution pairings. Periodic Green functions and boundary spectra, Theorems4.1–4.2, supplies complete integrable sampling and its continuous-representative proof; Theorem2.1 supplies one-dimensional periodic-distribution uniqueness. Bernoulli series and Poisson summation, Lemma0.1, proves finite positive-kernel uniqueness and smooth periodic expansion. The multidimensional version needed here is proved next. Spectral gaps and explicit Fourier distributions, Sections2 and4, supplies the Cauchy pair and finite sinc integral; its current Cauchy proof uses elementary half-line Laplace integration and Fourier inversion. Tempered growth and spectral cutoffs, Lemma2.1 and Theorem3.1, supplies the full Schwartz convolution and compact-spectrum fixed-point theorem. Separated frequencies and distributional order, Theorem3.1, proves strong exponential series and their whole atomic transforms in every dimension. The supplied Fourier foundation, F1–F5, scalar foundation, §§12–13, and integration foundation, §§15.0–15.4 and16, supply all inversion, Gaussian, calculus, convergence and integration inputs. Each supplied prerequisite retains its stated attribution and licence.

Periodic uniqueness in every dimension

Lemma0.1. Let and . A continuous function on , periodic with period in every coordinate, is determined by its Fourier coefficients A smooth such function has an absolutely convergent Fourier expansion with uniform convergence of every derivative. An arbitrary distribution periodic in these coordinates is determined by its periodic exponential pairings.

Proof for functions. Let be the one-periodic finite kernel proved in Bernoulli Lemma0.1. The product kernel is nonnegative and has integral one on , by finite product integration. Outside a fixed small coordinate neighborhood of , at least one coordinate is away from . The integral there is at most the sum of one-dimensional kernel tails; each tends to zero by the proved one-dimensional estimate. Uniform continuity of periodic therefore gives uniformly, by splitting its difference integral into that neighborhood and its complement. Expanding the finite product kernel shows that its convolution is the finite Fourier polynomial If all coefficients vanish, every polynomial vanishes and so does .

For smooth , repeated integration by parts on the periodic cube gives, with , All boundary terms cancel because opposite face derivatives agree. A dyadic shell contains at most lattice points, as its integer coordinates lie in a cube with that many points. Thus the differentiated Fourier series of order converges absolutely and uniformly if . The scalar fundamental theorem in each coordinate identifies all successive derivatives of the sum. Termwise integration and exponential orthogonality show that the sum has the coefficients of ; the preceding uniqueness proof identifies it with .

Proof for distributions. Rescale the one-dimensional compact smooth periodizing cutoff constructed in U057 Theorem2.1 from period to period ; its translates still sum to one. Take its product in all coordinates, obtaining with . Define for smooth periodic . Multiplication by this fixed compact cutoff is continuous from the periodic smooth seminorms to the compact-test topology, so this pairing is continuous. It is independent of the cutoff: if a compact smooth has zero periodization, insert the partition into , shift each term using periodicity, and obtain Only finitely many compact supports intersect before this shift. For every compact smooth , the same finite partition and shifts give The latter is smooth periodic; its sum is locally finite. If every periodic exponential pairing is zero, the smooth expansion just proved and continuity of give for every smooth periodic . The displayed identity then gives . Apply this to the difference of two distributions to obtain uniqueness.

4. Positive periodization of every bounded measurable input

Theorem 4.1. Fix , set , and let be a bounded measurable complex-valued representative on , with . Then converges absolutely, uniformly on compact sets in the sense of its uniformly vanishing tails. It is bounded by , measurable and -periodic. Its range lies in the closed convex hull of the range of . Its whole tempered Fourier support and exact pointwise error satisfy For an equivalence class these assertions hold almost everywhere with its essential bound and essential closed convex range. One may choose a representative taking all its values in the essential range and bounded by the essential supremum; then the literal pointwise assertions above hold. The resulting distribution is independent of changes to on a null set. No continuity of is assumed.

Proof of convergence, range and error. On a fixed compact -set the nonzero-index weights have a summable uniform bound, by the explicit tail of . Thus the series in (4.1) has uniformly small absolute tails. Reindexing proves periodicity. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one by Theorem 3.1. Any finite partial weighted sum, completed with its omitted weight at one fixed value in the range of , belongs to that convex hull; the omitted weight tends to zero and its values are bounded. Passing to the limit proves the closed-convex-hull assertion and the bound .

The zeroth weight is . Subtracting (4.1) from , using the sum of all weights equal to one, gives Its absolute value is bounded by times the omitted weights, which is exactly (4.3). For equivalence classes a common null exceptional set and its countably many translates suffice; outside their union every sampled value has the essential bound. Changes on a null set likewise change (4.1) only on such a countable translated union. The essential range is closed and lies in the bounded complex disk. All values belong to it off a null set: its open complement is a countable union of basis balls whose inverse images have measure zero. That exceptional union cannot cover a real interval, which also proves nonemptiness. Changing exceptional values to one fixed essential-range value supplies the stated bounded representative.

For a Schwartz test , define the compact-factor convolution by The inner function is Schwartz. Its every seminorm is bounded by times a fixed finite sum of seminorms of , because lies in one compact interval. This defines the tempered convolution on all tests.

Choose nonnegative compact smooth approximate identities , supported in , with integral one, and set . Then is compact smooth and tends to in , with one fixed compact support for . Now strongly in . Indeed bounded , the bound one on , and an integrable Schwartz weight give dominated convergence, uniformly on each bounded test family. On the other side the convolution test difference tends to zero in every Schwartz seminorm, at most times a finite test seminorm. The finite-order Schwartz bound for then proves strong convergence of its convolution, uniformly on bounded tests. Passing to the limit proves (4.4).

Let . The sum is closed: for any convergent sequence of sums, a subsequence of the compact-interval components converges; the other components then converge into the closed set . The support of is contained in this sum: if a compact test is supported outside it, its convolution test in (4.4) is compact smooth and supported away from . Hence its pairing is zero. Consequently , a continuous function, vanishes pointwise outside that set.

Finally (4.1) is precisely the -periodization of . Absolute unfolding gives its coefficients They are bounded by . The complete tempered exponential-series theorem Separated frequencies and distributional order, Theorem 3.1, applied to the integer lattice with and then scaled by , supplies the strongly convergent whole series and exact atomic transform. The series equals the periodization: their periodic pairings have the same coefficients, and the smooth periodic test expansion and partition argument proved in Periodic Green functions and boundary spectra, Theorem 2.1, show uniqueness. Thus Every atom outside has zero coefficient. The locally finite lattice has no other support points; alternatively pair any compact test in the complement with the entire atom series.
